stem: There are several mechanisms by which the rate of blood flow is regulated. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator and increases blood flow.
Blood flow increases in response to increased oxygen demand.
Blood flow increases as intracellular levels of calcium in endothelial cells increase.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

When endothelial cells have elevated intracellular calcium levels, the end-result is vasoconstriction. Vasoconstriction will increase blood pressure and reduce blood flow. Options A and B are both true.

weekLabel: Week 1 - Cardiac Physiology, ECG & Cardiac Pharmacology
lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following changes would result in the greatest change in blood pressure?

options.html: Doubling the rate of blood flow
Doubling the viscosity of the blood
Doubling the radius of blood vessels

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Changes in Pressure = Blood Flow * Resistance. By cutting the vessel radius in half, the vascular resistance is increased by 16-fold (since resistance is inversely proportional to r^4), and thus the change in pressure is also increased by 16 fold. Doubling the renal blood flow will also double the pressure change by as well. Doubling the vascular resistance will also double the change in pressure. Doubling the viscosity will double the vascular resistance and double the change in pressure. It’s important to know that the vessel radius is the most sensitive element influencing vascular resistance and thus influencing changes in pressure – which is why vessels contract and dilate to maintain blood flow to essential organs.

stem: Which of the following conditions/changes would NOT result in an increase in turbulent flow?

options.html: Arteriosclerotic plaques resulting in partial occlusions

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Factors that increase turbulence are an increase in blood velocity, vessel obstructions (occlusions), and a decrease in viscosity (a decrease in hematocrit). In conditions such as polycythemia vera where there is an increase in red blood cells, viscosity is increased thus we can expect a decrease in turbulence

stem: A patient presents to the ER with sudden traumatic blood loss occurring approximately 10 minutes ago. Which of the following changes can you expect to see in this patient?

options.html: An increase in atrial natriuretic peptide
An increase in aldosterone and angiotensin II
An increase in sympathetic nervous system output
An increase in parasympathetic nervous system output

answer:
The correct answer is D.

A sudden drop in blood pressure that comes from blood loss is mediated by the autonomic nervous system by increasing sympathetic output and decreasing parasympathetic output increasing the heart rate and contractility of the heart. A chronic drop in blood pressure is controlled by Vasopressin (ADH). ANP is a hormone secreted in response to a volume overload and promotes renal excretion of water. Angiotensin and Aldosterone also increase blood pressure through renal reabsorption of solutes and water, increasing volume and blood pressure however these are chronic responses to regulate blood pressure.

stem: Which of the following local changes will result in vasodilation of the vasculature? Select all that apply.

options.html: An increase in tissue oxygen consumption
Increased intracellular calcium in smooth muscle
Production of nitric oxide by eNOS

answer:
The correct answer is A, C.

An increase in oxygen consumption leads to the production of metabolites that can serve as vasodilators and dilate the local vasculature. Nitric oxide is a potent vasodilator. An increase in intracellular calcium leads to vasoconstriction. Angiotensin II can also act as a vasoconstrictor.

stem: What is the correct order of the three layers of the pericardium, from most superficial to most deep?

options.html: Fibrous pericardium -> Parietal pericardium -> Visceral pericardium
Fibrous pericardium -> Visceral pericardium -> Parietal pericardium
Parietal pericardium -> Visceral pericardium -> Fibrous pericardium
Parietal pericardium -> Fibrous pericardium -> Visceral pericardium
Visceral pericardium -> Parietal pericardium -> Fibrous pericardium
Visceral pericardium -> Fibrous pericardium -> Parietal pericardium

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The correct order of layers of the pericardium from most superficial to most deep is fibrous pericardium - parietal pericardium - visceral pericardium. The pericardial cavity is between the parietal and visceral pericardium.

stem: Which statement pertaining to the structure of the heart is true?

options.html: Blood enters the right atrium from the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and the great cardiac vein.
The three coronary arteries branch from the aorta.
Both right and left atria possess an auricle, however the left auricle is only visible posteriorly.
The tricuspid valves are tethered to papillary muscles via Chordae Tendineae.
The right ventricle generates a stronger contractive force than the left ventricle.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

This statement is true. Option A is false - the coronary vein that leads to the right atrium is the coronary sinus. Option B is false - the left and the right coronary arteries branch from the aorta, and the left coronary artery then further branches into the left anterior descending artery and the left circumflex artery. Option C is false - the left auricle is the only part of the left atrium visible anteriorly. Option E is false - the left ventricle generates a stronger contractive force.

stem: The heart contracts as a result of electrical conduction of nerve impulses beginning with the sinoatrial node. Which option below correctly lists the regions of the heart in order of electrical conduction?

options.html: Sinoatrial node -> AV Node -> AV Bundle -> Purkinje Fibers -> Bundle Branches
Sinoatrial node -> AV Node -> AV Bundle -> Bundle branches -> Purkinje Fibres
Sinoatrial node -> AV Bundle -> AV Node -> Purkinje Fibers -> Bundle branches
Sinoatrial node -> Purkinje Fibers -> AV Node -> AV Bundle -> Bundle branches
Sinoatrial node -> AV Bundle -> Bundle branches -> AV Node -> Purkinje Fibres

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The cardiac impulse begins at the SA node, followed by the AV node, the AV bundle (also called the bundle of His), then the left and right bundle branches, and finally the Purkinje fibers.

Sensory signals travelling retrograde along the Vagus nerves
Sensory signals travelling retrograde toward the C3-C5 spinal nerves
Sensory signals traveling retrograde along the phrenic nerves
Sensory signals travelling retrograde along the recurrent laryngeal nerves

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The sympathetic nerves that innervate the heart arise from the T1-T4/5 nerves. Referred pain in the thoracic cavity travels retrograde along the sympathetic nervous system.

options.html: Between the parietal pericardium and fibrous pericardium
Between the visceral pericardium and the myocardium
Between the parietal pericardium and visceral pericardium
Within the myocardium of the heart

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The fluid lies in the pericardial cavity which is the space between the visceral pericardium and the parietal pericardium.

stem: Transposition of the great vessels is the most common congenital heart lesion in neonates where the aorta and pulmonary trunk are transposed (so the left ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk and the right ventricle pumps blood into the aorta). Which of the following symptoms would be most prominent in a newborn infant with this condition?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Normally in newborn infants deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle and enters the pulmonary trunk into pulmonary circulation to get reoxygenated. In infants with this condition, blood leaves the right ventricle toward the aorta and back into circulation without oxygenation. Meanwhile oxygenated blood is received by the left ventricle (from the left atrium) and is pushed back into the pulmonary trunk and into pulmonary circulation. This condition requires surgical correction shortly after birth.

stem: Which of the following gives the best explanation of how atrioventricular valves open or close in the cardiac cycle?

options.html: When the ventricles relax the chordae tendineae emerging from the papillary muscle tense and close the valve
When the ventricles relax the chordae tendineae emerging from the papillary muscle pull and open the valve
When the ventricles contract the papillary muscles also contract, tensing the chordae tendineae and closing the valve
When the ventricles contract the papillary muscles also contract, tensing the chordae tendineae and open the valve

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The atrioventricular valves close at the beginning of isovolumetric contraction when the ventricles are contracting, which lead to the valves closing.

stem: Which of the following arteries will anastomose to supply the majority of the right and left ventricle and the interventricular septum?

options.html: The left anterior descending artery and the circumflex artery
The circumflex artery and the posterior interventricular artery
The left anterior descending artery and the posterior interventricular artery
The posterior circumflex artery and the left anterior descending artery

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The left anterior descending artery branches of the left coronary artery and runs in the anterior interventricular groove to supply the right ventricle, left ventricle and interventricular septum and anastomose with the posterior interventricular artery which runs in the posterior interventricular groove and supplies the same area.

stem: The lymphatic system displays a high degree of compliance. What does this mean?

options.html: A large volume increase corresponds to a small interstitial pressure increase.
A large volume increase corresponds to a large interstitial pressure increase.
A small volume increase corresponds to a small interstitial pressure increase.
A small volume increase corresponds to a large interstitial pressure increase.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Compliance is calculated as the change in volume divided by the change in pressure. The lymphatic system is able to accommodate a large volume increase with only a slight increase in interstitial pressure.

stem: Which of the following terms best describes the phenomena of red blood cells (RBCs) separating from the plasma and travelling through capillaries after bifurcation from the vasculature?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Plasma skimming involves the separation of RBCs from the plasma at junction of capillaries and travelling through in single file motion. Bulk flow is the movement of blood through relatively large arteries. Fick Principle states that uptake and secretion at the capillary level is a function of blood flow and the change in pressure from the arterial to venous side. RBC deformability is the ability of RBCs to change shape in response to external forces.

stem: If a patient has right ventricular hypertrophy, what observation would be expected in a 12- lead ECG?

options.html: A large R wave in lead V1
A large R wave in lead V5
A large T wave in lead aVR
A large T wave in lead aVF

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Right ventricular hypertrophy is associated with a large R wave in leads V1, V2, and V3. Left ventricular hypertrophy is associated with a large S wave in V1 and a large R wave in V6.

stem: If a patient’s ECG shows abnormalities in leads II, III, and lead aVF, which of the following is a reasonable interpretation?

options.html: There is an error in the ECG reading
There is an abnormality in the anterior portion of the heart
There is an abnormality in the inferior portion of the heart
There is an abnormality in the lateral portion of the heart

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Leads II,III and lead aVF all have at least one component of their vector which point down (inferiorly). Thus an abnormality in those leads may suggest an abnormality in the inferior portion of the heart.

stem: A recent heart attack survivor presents to the clinic for his 6-month follow-up. The patient seems to be doing well and is on his way to recovery. Which of the following pathologic signs would you expect to see in this patient’s ECG today?

options.html: There should be no abnormalities given the patient is currently healthy.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Q waves are persistent even after a patient has recovered from a heart attack and will be persistent on future ECGs. ST elevation signals a current myocardial infarction. ST depression and T wave inversion are indicative of ischemia.

stem: Consider the ECG below for a patient with complete (third-degree) AV-block. Which statement regarding the 12-lead ECG below is true?

options.html: The heart rate is above 60 bpm
Leads I, II, and aVF demonstrate right-axis deviation
There is a regular P wave

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The heartbeat is regular at about 50 bpm. With positive signals in leads I, II, and lead aVF, this is a normal axis ECG. Careful analysis of the rhythm strip indicates regular P waves and slower (but also regular) QRS waves characterized by complete (third-degree) AV block.

stem: Sildenafil was originally developed by Pfizer for the treatment of hypertension and angina. During its clinical trials, researchers discovered that the drug was more effective at inducing erections than treating angina, and thus, Viagra was born. What is the mechanism by which Viagra induces penile erections?

options.html: Viagra inhibits the enzyme that converts GTP to cGMP.
Viagra decreases the intracellular concentration of calcium in endothelial cells.
Viagra inhibits the enzyme that breaks down cGMP.
Viagra increases the cellular concentration of nitric oxide.
Viagra blocks the release of aldosterone from the adrenal glands.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Viagra works by preventing the breakdown of cGMP, a vasodilator. It does this by inhibiting phosphodiesterase-5, the enzyme that converts cGMP into GMP.

stem: Bradykinin is a vasodilator that, in excess amounts, can lead to a cough and edema of the tongue and airways. Which drug prescribed for hypertension is most likely to increase blood concentrations of bradykinin?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Angiotensin-II is a vasoconstrictor and stimulates the release of aldosterone from the adrenal glands. In addition to this, angiotensin II degrades bradykinin. ACE-inhibitors such as benazepril prevent the formation of angiotensin II, leading to elevated levels of bradykinin.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic after recovering from a myocardial infarction. The patient has chronic hypertension and has a respiratory illness which makes them particularly susceptible to pulmonary edema and coughing. Which of the following medications would you prescribe this patient to manage their cardiac condition?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

ACE-inhibitors and ARBs are both indicated in patients with hypertension and postmyocardial infarction. However, ACE-inhibitors prevent the metabolism of bradykinin, which leads to coughing and airway edema. In addition, a combination of ACEi’s and ARBs do not show clinical benefit but increase the risk of adverse events.

stem: Which of the following clinical signs can be expected to see in a patient with aortic stenosis? Choose as many as applicable

options.html: Diastolic murmur with an S3 sound
Systolic murmur with an S4 sound

answer:
The correct answer is B, D, G, H.

Aortic stenosis manifests as a systolic murmur with an accompanying S4 sound in late diastole. A shrunken valve area is indicative of aortic stenosis. Aortic stenosis can result in left ventricle hypertrophy as a result of an increase in the afterload. Angina and Syncope are common symptoms of aortic stenosis – angina can stem from ischemia (lack of myocardial perfusion from LV hypertrophy and reduced diastolic time) and syncope with exercise. In patients with aortic stenosis, their carotid pulse will be delayed and will be weak (pulsus parvus and tardus).

stem: 2. Johanna is a 77-year-old patient coming to your clinic. For the past three years, she has been noticing increasing shortness of breath and fatigue, especially after climbing stairs. Her blood pressure is 170/80, and during a physical exam, you hear a diastolic murmur. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The presence of a widened blood pressure range (the range between diastole and systole) in addition to a diastolic murmur strongly indicates aortic regurgitation. A patient with aortic regurgitation can also present with dyspnea following exertion.

stem: A patient arrives in your clinic concerned of chest pains. During the patient history, the patient admits to eating a lot of fast food. Based on clinical suspicion, you decide to obtain a more detailed image of the coronary arteries and coronary vessels. Which of the following tests should the physician order?
answer: Cardiac CT’s provide a detailed picture of cardiac vessel anatomy and can pinpoint calcifications and occlusions. It has comparable performance to that of an invasive angiogram. Echocardiography would not give any direct information about the coronary arteries. It may give indirect information through demonstration of wall motion abnormality that would imply either a severely stenosed or completely occluded vessel. MIBI scan would be helpful in demonstration of ischemia but otherwise would not give detailed information about the presence or absence of coronary disease. Cardiac MRI also provides excellent image resolution and is the test of choice for function and volume assessment when detailed information is required but CT would give better assessment of the coronary vasculature.

stem: The image below represents the jugular venous pressure throughout the cardiac cycle for a patient with cardiac tamponade (a wave=atrial contraction, x descent =atrial emptying, v wave= ventricular contraction, y descent= ventricular filling). Which of the following components of the image are abnormal relative to a healthy patient?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

In patient with cardiac tamponade, ventricular filling is compromised as pericardial effusions extrinsically compress the ventricle making it difficult to fill the ventricle. This is reflected on the Jugular venous pressure as a blunted y-wave.

stem: Which of the following invasive imaging modalities provide physicians the ability to treat the pathology while conducting the imaging test?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Cardiac catheterization involves placing a long rubber tube into your radial/femoral artery which enters your heart (ventricle, aorta, coronary arteries), and can simultaneously also be used for treatment (widening a narrowed artery). Transthoracic echocardiography and Nuclear scintigraphy are not invasive tests and do not offer any direct treatment. Transesophageal echocardiography does not directly facilitate treatment but may be used to guide treatments (for example closure of an atrial septal defect or MitraClip that are both performed through the circulatory system but guided by TEE).

stem: 6. Which of the following cardiac changes would you expect to see in a patient with constrictive pericarditis during inspiration?

options.html: A rise in jugular venous pressure and the interventricular septum bowing into the left ventricle
A rise in jugular venous pressure and the interventricular septum bowing into the right ventricle
A fall in jugular venous pressure and the interventricular septum bowing into the right ventricle
A fall in jugular venous pressure and the interventricular septum bowing into the left ventricle

answer:
The correct answer is A.

With inspiration there is negative thoracic pressure which draws venous return into the heart. In patients with pericardial constriction, the RV can’t expand laterally to accommodate the fluid volume so the septum bows into the left ventricle to increase the volume of the right ventricle. The rise in JVP can be attributed to the limited right ventricular filling which transmits blood back into the venous system leading to the visible distention (Kussmaul’s sign).

answer:

stem: Which condition is most consistent with an ECG that reveals QRS waves of alternating intensity?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

In pericardial effusion leading to tamponade, compression of the heart leads to the heart “swinging” within the pericardium. This swinging leads to electrical alternans, where QRS waves alternate in signal intensity.

stem: Which of the following best explains the etiology of rheumatic fever-induced mitral stenosis?

options.html: A streptococcal infection in the body leads to the production of antibodies, which also target cardiac valves (due to similarity in antigen structure) leading to inflammation and scarring

A streptococcal pathogen that creates an infection in the pharynx, eventually spreads to the pericardium and leads to an inflammatory response within the valvular structure leading to fibrosis and scarring
A streptococcal pathogen within the pericardium which produces a toxin that degrades the lining of the mitral annuluses
A streptococcal pathogen invades the pericardium and contributes to the coagulation of the blood which get deposited on the lining of the valves

answer:
The correct answer is A.

A streptococcal infection leads to the production of antibodies against a particular antigen on the pathogen, which is molecularly similar to an antigen in the valvular structure of the heart. Thus, the antibodies also mount an autoimmune response against the valves which leads to inflammation and scarring of the valves.

stem: While performing an echocardiogram for a patient suspected to have aortic regurgitation, you also notice a pathology associated with the mitral valve. How can mitral valve stenosis and mitral valve regurgitation be differentiated? Select all that apply.

options.html: Volume of cardiac output Presence of Pulmonary edema

answer:
The correct answer is A, B.

Mitral stenosis manifests as a diastolic murmur, while mitral regurgitation manifests as a systolic murmur. In Mitral stenosis right ventricular hypertrophy is more common as the pulmonary hypertension can transmit this pressure to the right ventricle and the RV can hypertrophy to compensate. In mitral regurgitation there is left ventricle hypertrophy to compensate for the reduced cardiac output and the volume overload. In mitral regurgitation and mitral stenosis there is reduced cardiac output (reduced stroke volume specifically), the presence of pulmonary edema and patients can report angina in both situations.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic with mitral stenosis. Which of the following conditions would you NOT commonly find in a patient with this disease?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

In mitral valve stenosis left atrium dilation is common as less blood is able to make it past the stenotic mitral valve and remains in the left atrium. The relative stasis of blood within the left atrium and lead to thrombus development. With the buildup of volume and pressure in the left atrium this can lead to a buildup of pressure in the pulmonary circulation. This additional pressure can also lead to hypertrophy of the right ventricle to compensate for the increased afterload. Additionally, because there is less blood entering the left ventricle, the left ventricle has less volume to pump into the systemic circulation so cardiac output is reduced.

Use the following clinical scenario to answer the next TWO questions.

Andrew is a 65-year-old man who presents to your walk-in clinic with dyspnea on exertion,

fatigue, and angina. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and regularly consumes alcohol.

When auscultating his heartbeat, you notice a systolic murmur loudest at the base, and the

presence of S4. Based on this presentation, you suspect aortic stenosis.

stem: What is the best test to confirm the diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Echocardiograms are diagnostic imaging tests for valvular diseases. A trans-thoracic echocardiogram would be preferred to a trans-esophageal echocardiogram because the transthoracic cardiogram is non-invasive.

stem: After confirming the diagnosis, you discuss with Andrew the different treatment options. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Andrew will require anticoagulation therapy to prevent thrombosis if he chooses a mechanical valve replacement.
If Andrew chooses a bioprosthetic valve replacement, his new valve will be very durable and likely will not need replacement.
Even with the valve replacement surgery, Andrew’s prognosis for survival is 5 years
Andrew’s symptoms will be alleviated with diuretics and other anti-hypertensive agents

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Mechanical valve replacements require anticoagulation therapy to prevent thrombosis. Bioprosthetic valves have a life-expectancy of 15 years. Prognosis for survival of aortic stenosis is 5 years after the development of angina symptoms; however, this is without surgical replacement of the aortic valve. Lastly, there is no medication currently available to address the symptoms of aortic valve stenosis.

answer:
The correct answer is A, B.

Diuretics are appropriate for patients with a normal sinus rhythm as this will reduce preload on the heart and relieve pulmonary congestion. Beta Blockers (reduce HR and increase diastolic filling time) and anticoagulants are indicated for patients with atrial fibrillation. Balloon valvuloplasty is an invasive procedure.

stem: Which of the following is an appropriate management option for a patient with aortic stenosis who has recently started experiencing angina?

options.html: No treatment is available for this condition
Monitor patient for the development of dyspnea and if developed consider an aortic valve replacement
Bioprosthetic valve replacement with oral anticoagulation (Warfarin)
Mechanical valve replacement with oral anticoagulation (Warfarin)

answer:
The correct answer is D.

In symptomatic patients (patients with angina, syncope, dyspnea), valve replacement is indicated as survival diminishes with the onset of symptoms. The life expectancy after the onset of angina is five years. Patients who receive a bioprosthetic valve replacement do not need oral anticoagulation; however this is necessary for patients with a mechanical valve replacement.

stem: You are seeing a patient complaining of chest pain. After a comprehensive patient history and physical exam, you suspect mitral valve stenosis. Which observation is inconsistent with this working diagnosis?

options.html: The patient has chest pain from pulmonary hypertension.
The patient’s heartbeat includes a diastolic murmur.
The patient has arthritis and a rash on his skin.
The patient’s ECG indicates atrial fibrillation.
The patient has left ventricular hypertrophy.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

In mitral valve stenosis, narrowing of the mitral valve would result in reduced volume supplied to the left ventricle. This would not lead to left ventricular hypertrophy.

stem: Andrew is a 65-year-old man who presents to your walk-in clinic with dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and angina. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and regularly consumes alcohol. When auscultating his heartbeat, you notice a systolic murmur loudest at the base, and the presence of S4. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the physical exam?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

A systolic murmur loudest at the base could be aortic stenosis, atrial septal defect, or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Of these three, only aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may demonstrate presence of S4. These two can be further differentiated by palpation: a triple apex beat on palpation is present in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

stem: Which of the following clinical signs are common in both aortic stenosis and chronic aortic regurgitation? Select all that apply.

options.html: Treatment only recommended in symptomatic patients

answer:
The correct answer is B, E.

In aortic stenosis (AS) and chronic aortic regurgitation (AR) left ventricular hypertrophy is common. In AS the increased afterload leads to ventricular hypertrophy while in AR the volume overload leads to Left ventricle hypertrophy and dilation. Both AR and AS are diagnosed through echocardiogram. Aortic Root enlargement is a common cause of AR. AS manifests as systolic murmurs while AR manifests as diastolic murmurs. Widened pulse pressure (the pressure between systolic and diastolic pressure) is characteristic of AR. For asymptomatic patients with AS, treatment is not indicated but for some asymptomatic patients with AR who have a dilated or failing left ventricle an operation is indicated.

stem: Which of the following management options is suitable for an elderly patient with severe aortic stenosis who also requests a minimally invasive option?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

There is no medical therapy available for Aortic Stenosis, which leaves SAVR and TAVI. Although TAVI is a minimally invasive option with short-term survival rates that are comparable with SAVR, long-term outcomes are thus far unknown. Minimally-invasive SAVR options exist (mini-sternotomy, mini-thoracotomy) for patients expected to live more than 5 years, allowing patients to have a more durable option with a lesser-invasive approach than a conventional sternotomy.

stem: You are a third-year medical student doing a rotation in the emergency department. Your patient is Saul, who presented with rapid-onset severe chest pain. Heartbeat auscultation reveals a systolic murmur, best heard at the apex. Suspecting a pathology associated with the heart valves, you perform a bed-side echocardiogram. Based on the clinical presentation, which diagnosis is the echocardiogram most likely to reveal?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

A patient with mitral regurgitation presents with a systolic murmur loudest at the apex. Acute mitral regurgitation is sudden in onset and leads to a presentation of pulmonary edema. This can be caused by endocarditis.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT true?

options.html: The “MitraClip” is an emerging therapy used to treat selected patients with mitral regurgitation
In general, there are more benefits to doing complete valve replacement over valve repair
In most scenarios stenotic valves must be replaced
Bioprosthetic valves in older individuals last longer than bioprosthetic valves in younger individuals
Patients with mechanical valves must stay on lifelong anticoagulation

answer:
The correct answer is B.

There are significant advantages to repairing a repairable valve over replacing the entire valve. There is increased durability, decreased risk of infection, thrombosis, thromboembolism, and less bleeding complications.

stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for aortic stenosis?

options.html: Rheumatic fever leading to aortic valve scarring

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Old age, congenital bicuspid aortic valve, and rheumatic fever that leads to scarring are all risk factors for aortic stenosis. An increase in dietary calcium is not a risk factor.

stem: A patient suffers from a mitral valve defect that requires immediate surgical intervention. Which statement accurately describes a limitation of mitral valve repair?

options.html: Mitral valve repair is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis relative to mitral valve replacement.
Mitral valve repair is associated with a decreased risk of survival relative to mitral valve replacement.
Mitral valve repair is not possible in some cases, such as mitral valve stenosis.
Patients with mitral valve repair are at increased risk of valvular infection relative to patients with a mitral valve replacement.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In general, mitral valve repair is preferred over mitral valve replacement, whenever mitral valve repair is possible. Mitral valve repair is not possible in cases of mitral valve stenosis. For example, mitral valve repair durability is inferior in most cases of stenosis due to rheumatic valve disease, and therefore replacement is preferred.

stem: Which of the following descriptions give the best explanation to how the S4 sound arises?

options.html: There is a rush of blood early in diastole that falls into a volume loaded ventricle
Blood rushes into a stiff/non-compliant ventricle late in diastole
The tricuspid and mitral valves close

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The S3 sound arises early in diastole as blood rushes in from the atria into the volume loaded ventricle. The S1 sound gives rise to the tricuspid/mitral valves closing at the beginning of systole. The S2 sound gives rise to the aortic/pulmonary valves closing at the end of systole.

stem: Which of the following causes of aortic regurgitation do NOT usually lead to left ventricle hypertrophy?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Rheumatic fever is a cause of acute aortic regurgitation, where enough time usually does not pass for left ventricle hypertrophy to develop. The leaflets of the aortic valve can deteriorate causing a backflow of blood into the left ventricle.

stem: Options for heart valve replacement include mechanical valves and bioprosthetic valves. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Mechanical valves are indicated in patients with a short life expectancy.
Bioprosthetic valves are contraindicated for patients who cannot tolerate anticoagulant therapy.
Bioprosthetic valves are more prone to deterioration than mechanical valves.
Patients with bioprosthetic valves are more prone to thrombosis relative to patients with mechanical valves.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Mechanical valves are much more durable than bioprosthetic ones; however, they require the patient to be maintained on warfarin anticoagulation therapy with associated risk of bleeding and thromboembolism. Thus, mechanical valves are contraindicated if a patient cannot tolerate anticoagulation therapy.

stem: A patient presents to the ER with severe chest pain, sweating and fatigue. Their ECG shows ST elevation, and therefore a diagnosis of STEMI is made requiring urgent management. Considering the resources available at the hospitals below, which immediate intervention should be administered to save the patient?

options.html: In a hospital without access to a catheterization lab, the patient should receive thrombolytic therapy with Tenecteplase administered intravenously.
In a hospital without access to a catheterization lab, the patient should receive Beta- Blockers and ACE-inhibitors administered orally.
In a hospital with access to a catheterization lab, the patient should receive thrombolytic therapy with Tenecteplase administered intravenously.
In a hospital with access to a catheterization lab, the patient should undergo coronary angiography.

answer: establish reperfusion, however this is only possible if there is a catheterization lab available at the hospital. In the absence of this, patients must undergo thrombolytic therapy for reperfusion. Beta-blockers and ACE-inhibitors are used to treat NSTEMI for their anti-ischemic effects. Coronary angiography is indicated for patients with NSTEMI, and is performed within 24-48 hours of the MI to view the vasculature and perform a PCI or surgery to revascularize. (NOTE there is a difference between coronary angiography and coronary angioplasty.)

stem:
Which of the following options best describes the order of intervention and assessment for a patient who enters the ER with a suspected MI? The patient’s vitals have already been checked.

  1. Conduct initial assessment and diagnose STEMI
  2. Provide aspirin
  3. Reperfusion through PCI/Thrombolysis
  4. Provide nitroglycerine/Beta-blockers and morphine if indicated
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The correct order of intervention involves addressing the patient’s vitals, providing Aspirin, then making a diagnosis of STEMI (through patient presentation and a 12 lead ECG), selecting a reperfusion strategy and then medication appropriate for the patient based on their history.

stem: Which of the following are validated management options to be used in the patients who have suffered from an acute myocardial infarction? Select all that apply.
answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C, D, E.

All of these options are well-established options of preventing further complications including another myocardial infarction or stroke in patients post-MI. Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) is often a lifelong therapy.

answer:
The correct answer is A, C, E, F, G.

Mitral stenosis, aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis, and atrial septal defect are not recognized as complications emerging from a myocardial infarct.

stem: After a myocardial infarction, patients may develop arrhythmic complications or pericarditis. Which option below incorrectly describes a treatment for such a complication?

options.html: If a patient develops an AV block, a pacemaker is installed in the patient.
If a patient develops ventricular fibrillation, beta-blockers are prescribed.
If a patient develops ventricular tachycardia, a pacemaker is installed in the patient.
If a patient develops post myocardial infarct pericarditis, general treatment is aspirin and colchicine.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Ventricular tachycardia following a myocardial infarct is treated with beta blockers or amiodarone to reduce the rate of ventricular contraction.

stem: Taylor and Drake have both suffered from an acute MI recently and as a part of their followup an echocardiogram was taken to assess for any complications. Taylor’s echocardiogram is shown on the left and Drake’s echocardiogram is shown on the right. Taylor’s heart did not have any ventricular rupture however showed transmural necrosis across the apex ventricular wall. Drake’s heart did have ventricular rupture however the pericardium was still intact. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: Taylor has a left ventricle aneurysm and Drake has a left ventricle pseudoaneurysm
Taylor has a left ventricle pseudoaneurysm and Drake has a left ventricle aneurysm
Taylor has a left ventricle free wall rupture and Drake has a left ventricle pseudoaneurysm
Taylor has a left ventricle pseudoaneurysm and Drake has a left ventricle free wall rupture

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Taylor’s echocardiogram is indicative of a left ventricle aneurysm where you can see a “wide neck” in the image, and all 3 layers (endocardium, myocardium, pericardium) are affected, however there is no rupture but a bulging at the apex of the heart. Drake’s echocardiogram is indicative of a left ventricle pseudoaneurysm, with a “narrow neck”. Furthermore, the pericardium is still intact and blood pools within this area. A free wall rupture would involve blood flowing into the pericardial sac.

stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for atherosclerosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Female sex is not a risk factor for atherosclerosis – male sex is a risk factor for atherosclerosis. Estrogen provides a protective effect against the development of atherosclerotic plaques.

stem: Which of the following aneurysms have an etiology that stems from atherosclerosis or inflammation?

options.html: Saccular aneurysm in the thoracic aorta
Fusiform aneurysm in the abdominal aorta

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Berry aneurysms in cerebral vessels are not related to atherosclerosis or inflammation. Their etiology is not well understood but it is believed to be an inherent weakness within the cerebral vessels and can rupture from transient increase in blood pressure.

stem: Which of the following pathologies does NOT require an invasive intervention?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Type B aortic dissections are dissections that begin within the descending aorta and only involve the descending aorta, and these dissections are usually managed with medications (blood pressure control). Type A aortic dissections require surgery and ruptured aneurysms also involve surgery with stent placement and sewing up the ruptured area.

stem: Complete the following sentence: Arterial dissection is the result of _______ of/on the arterial lining.
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The dissection of blood vessels arises directly from intimal entrance tears, where high pressure blood can enter the wall of the vessel and travel along the wall “splitting” the layers of the arterial lining. The etiology of intimal entrance tears is not well understood, but it is believed that hypertension leads to these small tears in the wall.

stem: Which of the following statements is false regarding aneurysms?

options.html: Aneurysms are more likely to be found around the bifurcation of the vessel
True aneurysms involve a dilation of all layers of the vessel wall
Aneurysms are typically found in areas of laminar blood flow
Aneurysms can harbour the development of thrombi

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Aneurysms are likely found in areas of turbulent blood flow (not areas of laminar flow), which explains why they occur around the bifurcations of blood vessels or in sharp turns of vessels. A true aneurysm involves all layers of the vessel wall expanding while false aneurysms involve the outer layer of the vessel dilating and pooling blood while the inner layers are intact. Aneurysms can harbor the development of thrombi, as blood can become stagnant within these dilations and begin to clot.

options.html: Double Vessel Disease with proximal LAD

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Left main coronary stenosis occurs when there is a 50% (or greater) reduction in the lumen of the left coronary artery and often carries the worst outcomes.

stem: Which of the following complications of Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery does not increase a patient’s mortality?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Neurocognitive changes do not increase a patient’s mortality, and these changes tend to resolve within 6 years. Cerebrovascular accident (which can result from an emboli), mediastinitis, and hemorrhage (with increasing need for transfusion) are all associated with increased mortality.

stem: Which statement regarding coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery is true?

options.html: During CABG surgery, the heart is injected with a high sodium solution to pause the heartbeat.
CABG surgery with the internal thoracic artery is associated with increased mortality relative to CABG surgery with the saphenous vein.
The estimated overall mortality of CABG is 2-3%, but mortality is higher in older patients.
CABG surgery increases short-term survival of patients (0-5 years), but medical treatments are more effective long-term (5+ years).

answer:
The correct answer is C.

As of 2001, the mortality associated with CABG surgery is overall 2-3%. The heartbeat is paused with an injection of high potassium solution. The internal thoracic artery is the best artery to use for long-term survival. Finally, CABG is ideal for long-term management of heart disease, whereas survival benefit associated with medical treatment is superior only in the short-term (0-1.5 years).

stem: A 65-year-old patient that is relatively healthy asides from having a myocardial infarction three years ago presents to the ER. They present with muscle weakness and severe pain in their lower left leg that is pale and cold. The physician assesses their lower right leg and can find a strong pulse but can’t find one in the lower left leg. Furthermore, this patient’s case file does not indicate any previous lower limb concerns. Which of the following pathologies is most likely causing these new symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The patient likely has an acute pathology as his presentation is sudden and he has not experienced lower limb concerns (claudication) in the past. An acute embolic ischemia is more likely to have normal contralateral pulses but not in the ipsilateral leg suggesting this patient does not have chronic peripheral vascular disease – thus there aren’t plaques obstructing the pulse in both legs. An abdominal aneurysm can harbor thrombi that can break off and travel downstream and clog femoral/popliteal/tibial arteries, leading to this condition; however, a cardiac source is the most common (namely atrial fibrillation).

Use the following passage to answer the next TWO questions.

A 70-year-old patient presents to your clinic with leg pain in both calves. The patient explains

the pain has been persistent over the past 6 months but it’s only noticeable when he does

laborious tasks such as mowing the lawn or shoveling the snow. Other than a few instances the

patient does not describe this as a large hindrance in his life. The patient lives a sedentary life, he

is a chronic smoker, and a recent lipid panel indicated hyperlipidemia.

stem: Which of the following pathologies is most likely causing these symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

These patient’s symptoms align with intermittent claudication – there is pain in his calf that is brought upon by exertion and relieved by rest. This patient might have narrowing of both of his femoral arteries from atherosclerotic plaques.

stem: Which of the following management options are reasonable to explore with this patient? Select FOUR answers.
answer:
The correct answer is B, D, E, F.

For patients with intermittent claudication the focus should be on Antiplatelet therapy (prescribing Aspirin), Blood pressure control, Cholesterol management (prescribing Statins), Diabetes management, Exercise and smoking cessation – the acronym ABCDE’S is useful to remember these. Surgical bypass and percutaneous revascularization are usually not recommended for patients with this condition especially if it is not having a large impact on his life and can be managed without it. Watchful waiting is not appropriate in this condition as without behavior/pharmacology modification the atherosclerotic plaques can grow and his symptoms will get worse.

stem: A patient with ongoing tissue loss, gangrene and resting pain in their lower limbs presents to your clinic. After a thorough investigation the physician diagnoses the patient with chronic limb Ischemia. The physician and patient are deciding on a management option. Which of the following statements are accurate?

options.html: The physician should consider a surgical bypass surgery if the patient prefers a minimally invasive procedure
The physician does not need to consider medical therapy (exercise, antiplatelet therapy) as it’s not relevant for this patient’s pathology
The physician should consider a surgical bypass surgery with an autogenous vein graft for its high durability
The physician should consider a surgical bypass surgery if the patient has diabetes and is susceptible to chronic infections

answer:
The correct answer is C.

A surgical bypass surgery with an autogenous vein graft is very durable and can last up to 5 years (or more), whereas percutaneous revascularization is less durable. If the patient wants a minimally invasive procedure the physician should consider percutaneous revascularization. Also, a percutaneous revascularization should be considered if the patient has a risk of infection (has major tissue loss) as a surgical bypass graft can become infected and lead to complications including limb loss. Medical therapy and risk factor modification are still very important on top of selecting a surgical intervention for the patient.

stem: The normal diameter of the descending thoracic aorta is 2.5 cm, and the normal diameter of the abdominal aorta is 2 cm. Francisco is a patient who just received a CT scan to assess for bone lesions caused by multiple myeloma. During the CT scan, the radiologist noted that Francisco’s descending thoracic aorta had fusiform growth to a diameter of 3.4 cm, and his abdominal aorta had fusiform growth to a diameter of 3.2 cm. Which statement is true?

options.html: The descending aorta has an aneurysm and the abdominal aorta has an aneurysm
The descending aorta has an aneurysm and the abdominal aorta has ectasia
The descending aorta has ectasia and the abdominal aorta has an aneurysm
The descending aorta has ectasia and the abdominal aorta has ectasia

answer:
The correct answer is C.

An aneurysm is defined as a growth in diameter of more than 50% of the normal diameter. Growth less than 50% is defined as ectasia.

stem: Which of the following modalities is currently used to screen patients for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Ultrasounds are used to screen patients for abdominal aortic aneurysms. CT scans are the gold standard however they are also more expensive.

stem: Which of the patients below would not qualify for a screen for an abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.html: Albert, a 55-year old male with whose father died of an AAA rupture
Betsy, a 65-year old female with a 30 pack-year smoking history
Charlie, a 70-year old male without any symptoms
David, an 80-year old male whose previous AAA screen at age 65 was negative

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The current Canadian guidelines for AAA screening are a one-time ultrasound for men between ages 65 and 75, a one-time ultrasound for women with risk factors, or a one-time ultrasound for patients older than 55 with a family history. David is outside of the age range for screening and has already been screened negative.

stem: Bill is a 55-year-old patient who has been suffering from a severe chronic infection and was recently diagnosed with a mycotic abdominal aneurysm. The diameter of the aneurysm is 3.5 cm. The patient’s chronic infection has also deteriorated several of his organs. Which of the following management options is best suited for this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

For patients with a pseudoaneurysm or mycotic aneurysm there is a need to operate despite size as they grow faster and rupture at smaller sizes – even with antibiotic treatment. The endovascular repair is preferable to an open surgical repair, as it’s less invasive. Furthermore, given the patient’s existing infection and organ damage this makes him more susceptible to complications from an open surgical repair.

stem: Which of the following aneurysms would an endovascular repair be least appropriate?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Popliteal aneurysms are usually repaired with an open bypass operation, as endovascular repair is less frequently used due to the risk of occlusion. For suprarenal, juxtarenal and infrarenal aortic aneurysms, endovascular repair is indicated in most patients.

stem: Which statement below concerning aneurysm rupture is false?

options.html: Aneurysm rupture risk increases as the diameter of the aneurysm increases
Aneurysms remain stable or are degenerative - they never regress
Aneurysm rupture is associated with an overall 40-50% mortality rate
Aneurysms are repaired as prophylactic treatment to avoid rupture

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The overall mortality rate of an aortic aneurysm rupture is 80%. Among those who are able to make it to the hospital, the mortality rate is 40-50%. The rest of the statements are true.

stem: A patient has been experiencing worsening symptoms of pulmonary congestion and palpitations. A physician orders an echocardiogram which reveals cardiomegaly associated with eccentric cardiomyopathy anterolaterally. What is the likely diagnosis?

options.html: Left-sided heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Pulmonary congestion and palpitations are associated with left-sided heart failure. Eccentric cardiomyopathy indicates a volume-overloaded ventricle, consistent with leftsided HFrEF.

stem: A patient has been experiencing prolonged peripheral edema and upon physical examination it is noted that she has an elevated jugular venous pressure, and presence of ascites. Lung sounds are normal. What is the likely diagnosis?

options.html: Left-sided heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The absence of lung pathology and lung sounds indicates right-sided heart failure. Peripheral edema and elevated JVP are consistent with right-sided heart failure: with reduced blood outflow from the right ventricle, blood volume pools in the veins.

stem: A patient came into your clinic with some concerns of his health following his heart attack last year. He feels winded after climbing the stairs, and his partner has been complaining recently of his loud snoring. Suspecting heart failure, you order an echocardiogram, which reveals concentric hypertrophy. What is the likely diagnosis?

options.html: Left-sided heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Dyspnea on exertion and obstructive sleep apnea indicate left-sided heart failure, and concentric hypertrophy is associated with preserved ejection fraction.

stem: Sacubitril and valsartan when combined are an example of the ARNI class of heart failure medications. What is the mode of action of sacubitril? What is the mode of action of valsartan? Select TWO answers.

options.html: Sacubitril breaks down ANP, BNP, and CNP
Sacubitril inhibits the enzyme that breaks down ANP, BNP, and CNP.
Sacubitril inhibits the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
Valsartan inhibits the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
Valsartan blocks the binding of angiotensin II to receptors in the adrenal glands.
Valsartan blocks the binding of aldosterone to mineralocorticoid receptors in the kidneys

answer:
The correct answer is B, E.

An ARNI (angiotensin receptor / neprilysin inhibitor) includes valsartan as the angiotensin receptor inhibitor (blocks the binding of angiotensin II) and sacubitril (inhibits neprilysin). Neprilysin is an enzyme which catalyzes the break-down of natriuretic peptides such as ANP, BNP, and CNP.

stem: A 55-year-old patient who has persistent COPD presents to your clinic with ascites and severe swelling of the foot. Upon physical examination you to notice this patient has a distended jugular vein. You are suspecting heart failure; which of the following types of heart failure is most likely in this scenario?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Right-sided heart failure can arise from chronic lung diseases such as COPD, where there is an increase in pulmonary pressure. Increased pulmonary pressure leads to fluid back-up into the right ventricle and back into the venous system, which can manifest as a distended jugular vein. The blood can also pool into her extremities leading to edema of the foot and ankles. Although right sided hypertrophy can arise from left sided hypertrophy, in this scenario there are no unique symptoms that suggest this patient has diastolic/systolic left sided failure such as cyanosis, tachycardia and unexplained pulmonary congestion.

stem: “Heart A” and “Heart B” are both hearts from patients who had heart failure. Which of the following statements are likely true? Choose THREE answers.

options.html: Heart A likely belonged to a patient with systolic heart failure; Heart B likely belongedto a patient with diastolic heart failure
Heart B likely belonged to a patient with systolic heart failure; Heart A likely belongedto a patient with diastolic heart failure
Heart A shows concentric hypertrophy; Heart B shows eccentric hypertrophy
Heart B shows concentric hypertrophy; Heart A shows eccentric hypertrophy
The individual with Heart A likely experienced reduced ejection fraction, but theindividual with Heart B likely did not
The individual with Heart B likely experienced reduced ejection fraction, but theindividual with Heart A likely did not

answer:
The correct answer is B, C, F.

Heart A shows concentric hypertrophy where sarcomeres develop in parallel leading to increased ventricular wall thickness, and this is often the case in diastolic heart failure where the heart is unable to fill properly and there is increased afterload – ejection fraction does not diminish in this case due to the compensatory ventricular wall hypertrophy. Heart B shows eccentric hypertrophy where sarcomeres develop in series (the ventricular wall thickness remains the same) so the ventricle can dilate. This is often in response to systolic heart failure where the heart is unable to pump blood effectively, so blood accumulates in the ventricle (increased preload) and ejection fraction is decreased.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Heart Failure, Hypertension & Congenital Disease

stem: Which of the following statements regarding medications for heart failure is false?

options.html: IF channel inhibitors reduce the heart’s contractility and the heart rate
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists lower blood pressure by promoting diuresis
Beta Blockers play a significant role in reducing fibrosis and hypertrophy of the heart
ARNI plays a role in prolonging the effects of vasoactive peptides and by inhibiting theeffects of Angiotensin II

answer:
The correct answer is A.

IF channel inhibitors block the sodium/potassium channels in the SA node leading to a reduction in heart rate, however contractility is not impaired. Beta Blockers reduce both heart rate and contractility in addition to reducing hypertrophy and fibrosis.

stem: Despite treatment with heart failure medications, a 70-year-old patient with worsening left sided heart failure is now unable to go on his daily walks without feeling out of breath. Going up the stairs has also become an exhausting task for him. He has become more sedentary and spends his time watching TV on the couch. He says this is the only time he’s really comfortable. How would you classify this patient’s heart failure based on the New York Heart Association’s classification system?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Class III is when there is significant limitation in activity due to the symptoms, however the patient is comfortable at rest. Class IV is when the patient experiences symptoms at rest. Class I is when the patient has heart failure but no symptoms and no limitations on activities, while class II involves a mild limitation on activities.

stem: A 65-year-old patient presents to your clinic after recovering from a myocardial infarction. An echocardiogram has revealed the patient has a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 35%. The patient reports fatigue and chronic shortness of breath - they are having a difficult time performing any physical tasks, and even experience these symptoms while in bed or sitting down. After consulting with the patient, you create an appropriate treatment plan. One year later you follow up with the patient and they report feeling much better, they can perform household tasks and even take their dog for a walk with minimal symptoms. They no longer experience symptoms when in bed or are laying down. What is the current AHA /ACC stage of the patient’s heart failure and their functional class (New York Heart Association Classification)?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The patient’s functional class is level II, as they experience mild and bearable symptoms during physical activities, but they don’t experience symptoms at rest. The patient’s class prior to treatment was class IV as this patient experienced symptoms at rest and during physical activity. The patient’s stage of heart failure prior to treatment is at stage C where they have structural defects in the heart and are experiencing symptoms. Despite the fact their symptoms are reduced, this patient would still be classified as Stage C: Structural heart failure and current OR prior symptoms.

stem: Bill is a 79-year-old patient who suffered an anterior wall myocardial infarction three years ago. Despite rapid treatment, Bill was left with some mild damage to his heart. He has since managed quite well with aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin. Currently, he has never had any symptoms of heart failure and is able to do all his activities of daily living. At a recent check-up, his left ventricular ejection fraction was 45%. According to the ACC / AHA classification, NYHA classification, and the classification based on ejection fraction, how would you best classify Bill’s heart condition? Select THREE answers.
answer:
The correct answer is B, E, J.

ACC / AHA Stage B is associated with structural heart damage but no symptoms. NYHA is a functional classification, and since Bill is asymptomatic, he is NYHA Class I. With an ejection between 40% and 49%, this patient has heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction (HFMREF).

stem: Which of the following patients meet the clinical definition of Heart Failure? Select all that apply.

options.html: A 50-year-old patient who is at risk for coronary artery disease and does not experience any symptoms

A 51-year-old patient who has recently developed aortic regurgitation with an echocardiogram revealing left ventricular dilation with reduced ejection fraction but the patient does not experience any symptoms
A 52-year-old patient with severe aortic regurgitation and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction who chronically feels fatigued and out of breath
A 54-year-old patient who is currently hospitalized and has become increasingly frail after suffering from aortic regurgitation and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction.

answer:
The correct answer is C, D.

Option A represents Stage A in Heart Failure where there are no structural heart defects and no symptoms. Option B represents Stage B where the patient has a structural heart defect but no symptoms. Options C represents a patient with a structural heart defect and clear symptoms which meets the criteria for Heart Failure. Option D represents a patient in stage D who is suffering from advanced heart failure.

stem: Heart failure is associated with a myriad of symptoms with a large differential diagnosis. Which statement below on diagnostic tests for heart failure is true?

options.html: An ECG can diagnose valvular diseases and ventricular enlargement
An endomyocardial biopsy is a post-mortem pathological investigation
A Chest X-Ray provides information on heart size and status of pulmonary congestion and edema.
Elevated BNP levels are an indication of a pulmonary pathology.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This statement is true. Option A is false - ECGs provide information on previous and current myocardial infarctions but not valvular diseases. Option B is false - this is not a postmortem biopsy. Option D is false - elevated BNP levels are an indication of a cardiac pathology.

stem: Which of these patients are expected to have the worst prognosis upon presentation to a hospital with heart failure?

options.html: A patient with mental confusion and cold-sweated extremities
A patient with pulmonary congestion and jugular venous dilatation
A patient with cold extremities and pulmonary congestion
A patient with cold extremities only

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Cold extremities indicates hypoperfusion, associated with poorer prognosis, and pulmonary congestion is also associated with poorer prognosis. This patient would be classified as “cold and wet”. The patients in options A and D would be classified as “cold and dry”, and the patient in option B would be classified as “warm and wet”.

stem: The presence of which of the following signs/markers after a thorough investigation is enough to exclude a diagnosis of Heart Failure?

options.html: Low BNP levels within the blood
High BNP levels within the blood
Absence of Q waves on the ECG
A patient with an ejection fraction of 50%

answer:
The correct answer is A.

After conducting a through history, physical examination and completing the intial investigations (which can include an ECG, Chest X-ray, echocardiogram, and blood work), if the physician is still suspecting heart failure, they can rely on the patient’s BNP levels to exclude/include heart failure. If the patient has reduced BNP (<50 pg/ml) this can exclude a diagnosis of heart failure.

stem: Which of the following physiologic changes would you NOT expect to see in a patient with left-sided systolic heart failure?

options.html: Increased sodium retention in the kidneys

answer:
The correct answer is B.

In patients with left ventricular systolic heart failure the pumping efficiency is decreased so blood pools within the ventricle which can lead to ventricular dilation. In addition since the ejection fraction and cardiac output is reduced the body compensates for this by increasing blood pressure through sodium retention in the kidneys (which draws water back into systemic circulation increasing volume and pressure) and by vasoconstriction (which also increases blood pressure). Vasodilation is not expected to happen. Arrhythmias are possible when the heart becomes enlarged, this can disrupt the conduction system and lead to abnormal rhythms.

stem: Which of the following patients are suffering from restrictive cardiomyopathy?

options.html: A patient who suffered from myocardial infarction, which led to necrosis of their myocardium and ultimately dilation of the left ventricle with a resultant wall motion abnormality
A patient with long standing aortic regurgitation which has led to a dilated left ventricle with reduced ejection fraction
Significant hypertrophy of myocardium, possibly of a genetic etiology resulting in hypertrophied and a stiff ventricle.
A patient with enlarged atria and infiltration of the myocardium which has led to stiff ventricles (e.g., cardiac amyloidosis).

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is when the wall of the ventricles are stiff but not necessarily thickened. This can result from cardiac amyloidosis or be idiopathic. Commonly the atria are enlarged. Option C is an example of a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Option B is an example of a dilated cardiomyopathy with a valvular origin. Option A is an ischemic cause of a dilated left ventricle.

options.html: A contraindication for treatment with ARNIs is current treatment with ACE- inhibitors.
A contraindication for treatment with beta-blockers is bilateral renal arterial stenosis.
A contraindication for treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors is the presence of diabetes.
A contraindication for treatment with ivabradine (an If channel inhibitor) is sinus rhythm.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

stem: In 2019, dapagliflozin was approved for the treatment of heart failure. Dapagliflozin is a SGLT2 inhibitor that was originally approved for the treatment of diabetes. For which of the patients below is Dapagliflozin recommended? Select all that apply.

options.html: A patient with HFrEF and diabetes
A patient with HFrEF and no diabetes
A patient with HFpEF and diabetes
A patient with HFpEF and no diabetes

answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C.

Dapagliflozin is used to treat diabetes, so options A and C are correct. Data also suggests that Dapagliflozin is effective in the treatment of HFrEF even in patients without diabetes, making option B also correct.

stem: Which of the following combination treatments is currently recommended for initial management of patients with Heart Failure with reduced ejection fraction (<40%)?

options.html: Angiotensin Converting Enzyme inhibitor, Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
Angiotensin Converting Enzyme inhibitor, Beta-Blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
Angiotensin receptor / Neprilysin inhibitor, Beta-Blockers and mineralocorticoid receptors
Angiotensin receptor / Neprilysin inhibitor, Beta-Blockers and Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Initial management for these patients is triple therapy – ACEi (or ARB if the patient is intolerant to ACEi), Beta blockers and MRA. Patients should not be on both ACEi and ARBs. ARNI is introduced later in therapy for patients with NYHA classifications II-IV.

stem: Which of the following therapies primarily prevents sudden cardiac death for patients with heart failure?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Sudden Cardiac Death originates from arrhythmia. An ICD is implanted within a patient to prevent abnormal rhythms (ventricular arrhythmia specifically) that can lead to sudden cardiac death.

stem: Which patient below should be referred to advanced care for end-stage heart failure?

options.html: Abigail, whose heart failure is NYHA Class II with an ejection fraction of 30%
Brenda, who consistently has elevated BNP and has required 3 hospitalizations for heart failure in the past year
Corina, who has pitting edema and a blood pressure of 110/75.
Deborah, who wants a heart transplant despite good management with her current meds.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

For referral for advanced care, a patient should have two of the symptoms or signs in the I NEED HELP acronym. Abigail would qualify if her heart failure was NYHA Class III or IV and her ejection fraction was less than 20%. Corina would qualify if she had pitting edema and a low blood pressure of <90 mmHg (systole). Deborah has good management and would not qualify.

stem: Which statement concerning the care of advanced heart disease is false?

options.html: Even though a patient may feel better after cutting back on beta-blockers, this will not prolong their life.
In a heart transplant, the donor’s heart is usually connected to the recipient’s heart in series.
Common complications of a ventricular assist device are driveline infection and thrombosis.
In 50% of cases, a transplanted heart survives 12 years following transplantation.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Donor hearts are not connected in series to the recipient’s heart. The recipient’s heart is removed, and the donor heart is anastomosed with the patient's aorta, pulmonary veins, and venae cavae. The remaining options are true.

stem: Which statement on the variability of blood pressure (BP) is true?

options.html: A routine clinical BP measurement is likely to underestimate a patient’s BP.
For most accurate BP measurements, a patient should be sitting at rest for at least five minutes while discussing their patient history.
The best predictor of cardiovascular risk are BPs measured by highly trained nurses.
The gold standard for accurate BP measurements is an ambulatory BP measurement.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Option A is false - routine clinical BP typically measurements overestimate a patient’s BP by (on average) 9 mmHg. Option B is false - a patient should not be talking while taking a BP measurement. Option C is false - while nurses may have more training in taking BP measurements, a patient may still have “white coat hypertension”, in which their BP is elevated in a primary care office. Ambulatory BP measurement provides accurate BP measurements in a patient’s home environment.

stem: A patient comes to your clinic concerned they have high blood pressure after a close relative received that diagnosis. As the physician you take his blood pressure while he is sitting and still – the patient’s blood pressure is 160/100. Which of the following is an appropriate next step?

options.html: Diagnose the patient with hypertension and discuss next steps
Reassure the patient they don’t meet the threshold for hypertension
Reassure the patient they don’t have hypertension but ask them to follow up in 1 year
Arrange for an out of office assessment to be done (Ambulatory or Home Blood Monitor)

answer:
The correct answer is D.

In this scenario the patient’s blood pressure is below the 180/110 threshold to diagnose hypertension, but still significantly high to warrant further investigation. This can be done by arranging ABP or HBP. If the ABP is >135/85 or the HBP is >140/90 this is enough for further investigation to be done, where another ABP/HBP is taken 1 month after the visit.

stem: Felicia is a retired 72-year-old woman who was persuaded by some friends to invest in an athome blood pressure monitor. After recording her blood pressure at 180/115 mmHg, she approached her doctor for a prescription for anti-hypertensives. She is currently fighting off a bacterial pneumonia infection (with associated cough), blood tests reveal a low serum potassium level and physical exam indicates low blood volume. The physician is most likely to prescribe a low-salt diet, regular exercise, and which drug(s)? Select at most 2 answers.
answer:
The correct answer is B, E.

With a highly elevated blood pressure of 180 mmHg (systole), Felicia’s target BP is 140 mmHg (40 mmHg difference). With this large difference, Felicia’s first-line treatment should include two antihypertensive agents. She currently has a cough, so an ACE-inhibitor is contraindicated. She is over 60, so a beta-blocker is contraindicated (as a first line therapy). Finally, she is hypovolemic, so a diuretic is contraindicated. This leaves an ARB and a CCB.

stem: Clark is a 66-year-old patient with hypertension (BP 170/110 mmHg). Three months ago, his doctor prescribed both ramipril (an ACE-inhibitor) and indapamide (a diuretic). He has diligently taken all medication as prescribed, and today, his blood pressure is 155/104 mmHg. Assuming Clark is low risk, what would be the next course of action for Clark’s management?

options.html: Continue the current treatment – blood pressure takes more than 3 months to adjust following a medication change.
Double the current doses of ramipril and indapamide
Supplement the current medication regimen with candesartan (an ARB)
Supplement the current medication regimen with amlodipine (a CCB)

answer:
The correct answer is D.

If a patient has not completely responded to double-therapy, a third antihypertensive agent should be prescribed. For a patient on triple therapy, the drug classes are normally an ACE-inhibitor OR an angiotensin receptor blocker, a diuretic, and a calcium channel blocker.

stem: For a patient with severe hypertension, triple-therapy is recommended. How should a physician approach triple therapy for severe hypertension?

options.html: Prescribe one medication at a time, and check for symptoms continually before and after adding another medication
Prescribe one medication from the cocktail at a low dose, and then continue to increase that dose until you’ve reached maximal efficacy.
Prescribe all the medications at once at maximal dose and monitor for symptoms.
Prescribe all the medications initially in a combination pill at a moderate dose and monitor for symptoms as you reach the maximal dose

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Often it’s better to prescribe multiple medications at once, perhaps in a single pill, and then increase the dosage as you monitor for symptoms. Prescribing the medications one at a time, will eliminate the enhanced response that comes with combination therapy.

stem: Elizabeth is four weeks old. She was born following an uncomplicated pregnancy and returned to the hospital today due to cyanosis of the skin. Her parents also note that Elizabeth has sweats while feeding. A chest X-ray reveals increased pulmonary blood flow and a “snowman”-shaped heart. Based on this information, what is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Cyanosis with increased pulmonary flow as indicated by Chest X-ray could be truncus arteriosus or total anomalous pulmonary venous return. However, TAPVR is associated with a “snowman”-shaped heart on Chest X-ray. Elizabeth will need surgical intervention. Note that transposition of the great arteries can cause cyanosis with increased pulmonary blood flow, but this would present with severe cyanosis on the first day of life.

stem: Which of the following cyanotic congenital heart conditions does not have a completely curative surgery available?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Tricuspid atresia is the condition associated with an absent tricuspid valve. There are no curative surgeries available for this condition; however, some palliative surgeries exist to prolong life until early adulthood.

stem: Which of the following cardiac structures within a fetus is pathological?

options.html: A shunt between the right atrium and left atrium
A shunt between the right ventricle and left ventricle
A shunt that allows blood to bypass the liver
A shunt between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk

answer:
The correct answer is B.

A shunt between the right ventricle and left ventricle is a ventricular septal defect and is not a normal finding in a fetus. The foramen ovale is shunt between the right and left atrium. The ductus venosus is a shunt that allows blood to bypass hepatic circulation. The ductus arteriosus is a shunt between the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

stem: A 2-month-old child presents to your clinic with severe congestion. The baby appears to be well perfused and displays no signs of cyanosis. Further tests reveal increased pulmonary blood flow and a large left heart. A pansystolic ejection murmur is also heard. Which of the following pathologies best explains the patient’s symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The patient most likely has a ventricular septal defect. In VSD there is a shunting of blood from the left ventricle into the right ventricle, which leads to an equalization of pressure in the right and left ventricle. The increased volume in the right ventricle gets pumped into the pulmonary arteries which can lead to pulmonary edema. In ASD patients do not experience right and left ventricular pressure equalization. Coarctation of the aorta does not explain the increased pulmonary blood flow. Tetralogy of Fallot and Truncus Arteriosus would both result in cyanosis of the child.

stem: Within the first week of life a child presents mildly cyanotic. Upon examination the physician can hear a systolic ejection murmur. The following X-ray was obtained and the physician notes the lack of pulmonary blood flow, displayed by dark areas in the lung fields. Which of the following pathologies is the likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Tetralogy of Fallot is the likely diagnosis. In patients with this condition the entrance to the pulmonary trunk is narrowed/obstructed leading to reduced pulmonary flow. Furthermore, the VSD present allows for the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood leading to mild cyanosis in the patient. Right ventricular hypertrophy and an overriding aorta are also features of this pathology. The chest X-ray also displays the “boot” that is commonly associated with the Tetralogy of Fallot.
